data.title: <![CDATA[The Trends Reshaping the Healthcare Practice of Tomorrow: Q&A with Austin Strong]]>
data.description:
Pharmaceutical Executive spoke with Austin Strong, head of strategy at Weave, about what he expects the biggest trends in 2027 to be. The conversation focused on healthcare providers and how they engage both with patients and the pharmaceutical industry. How these trends play out will directly impact how the pharma and biotech industries must adapt their strategies to ensure their drugs make it to the patients that need them.

According to Strong, the next year will be focused on both affordability and improving the usage of new technologies, such as AI. While he discussed areas where he expects this technology to expand, he also discussed how decision-making in this area is likely to change as well.

Click for the video version of this interview!

Pharmaceutical Executive: How important will the issue of affordability of healthcare be in 2027?
Austin Strong: One of the big things we’re running into is that healthcare is getting a lot more expensive — even if you remove general inflation from the equation. One of the studies we’ve done found that workers are spending an average of around $7,500 to $8,000 annually on healthcare coverage. That’s almost 10% more than what they were paying in 2025.

What has been interesting is how insurance companies and employers have adapted: we’re seeing more and more healthcare practices adopt what we’re calling a flexible payments model. As Americans, we’re very familiar with this concept in other areas of our lives. When you purchase a car, you take out a loan and make monthly installments. If you see a nice pair of jeans online for $150, you can break that up into four smaller payments rather than paying all at once.

data.title: <![CDATA[Leading Takeda’s Plasma-Derived Therapies Business: Q&A with Ramy Riad]]>
data.description:
In a conversation with Pharmaceutical Executive, Ramy Riad, President of Takeda’s Plasma-Derived Therapies (PDT) Business Unit, discusses the strategic priorities shaping one of the company’s largest and fastest-growing businesses, emphasizing the balance between operational excellence, innovation, and the needs of donors and patients alike.

Riad describes the transition from his former role as CFO to President, noting that the broadened responsibility now spans the entire value chain, from plasma collection at Takeda’s BioLife centers through global manufacturing and delivery of therapies to patients. The conversation also covers Takeda’s efforts to diversify and strengthen the global plasma supply chain, including an investment of up to $30 million to help build a plasma ecosystem in Indonesia, the company’s first initiative of its kind.

Riad further addresses evolving and emerging applications for plasma-derived therapies, including secondary immunodeficiency and the company’s investigational candidate TAK-881, as well as Takeda’s partnerships with international organizations to improve diagnosis and access. He closes by discussing ongoing innovation efforts, from subcutaneous and home-administration treatment options to automation and AI-driven manufacturing improvements, all aimed at maximizing therapeutic benefit from every donation.

A transcript of Riad’s conversation with Pharmaceutical Executive can be found below.

Pharmaceutical Executive: You helped shape PDT’s strategy as CFO and now lead the business unit. What are your top priorities in this role and what looks different from your role as President of the organization? Has anything surprised you?
Ramy Riad: Having helped shape our strategy and operating model as CFO, stepping into my role as President of the Plasma-Derived Therapies (PDT) Business Unit felt like a natural progression. Our business differs from traditional pharmaceuticals as we produce critical medicines made from proteins in donated human plasma. These therapies are used to treat people with rare and complex chronic conditions, including immunodeficiencies, where PDTs are often the only viable treatment option and the demand continues to grow.

data.title: <![CDATA[The Role of Automation and AI in Medication Management and Resident Care]]>
data.description:
As America's Baby Boomer generation ages, long-term care providers face a growing challenge: meeting increasingly complex medication needs with a workforce already under pressure. For pharmaceutical companies and healthcare providers, the question is not simply how to develop effective medications, but how to ensure those therapies reach patients reliably and safely.

Having spent more than two decades building a long-term care pharmacy business, I have seen firsthand how much coordination goes into getting medications to residents. Medication management involves far more than filling prescriptions. It requires precise dispensing, packaging, sorting, delivery, and communication among pharmacies, prescribers, and care teams.

That experience has reinforced my belief that automation and artificial intelligence (AI) must play a larger role in helping the industry manage growing demand without proportionally increasing manual work.

Automation Is Reshaping Medication Management

Traditional pharmacy operations involve numerous repetitive steps, from selecting and packaging medications to labeling, verification, sorting, and preparing orders for delivery. At scale, these tasks create substantial operational demands.

My experience investing in pharmacy automation has shown me how technology can help standardize these processes. Single-dose dispensing robotics and automated packaging systems can handle repetitive tasks with greater consistency, while barcode verification and electronic tracking can improve visibility into medication workflows.

The objective is not to eliminate human involvement. It is to reduce unnecessary manual handling and create more reliable processes, allowing pharmacists and technicians to focus on clinical questions, exceptions, and quality oversight.

data.title: <![CDATA[FDA Misses Deadline on Savara’s Rare Lung Disease Drug, Leaving Approval Timeline Open]]>
data.description:
The US Food and Drug Administration has told Savara Inc. it will not meet its November 22, 2026 target date for a decision on the company’s biologics license application for molgramostim inhalation solution — a potential first-in-class treatment for autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, a rare and progressive lung disease with no currently approved therapies.

Savara disclosed the news on November 20, stating that the FDA’s review remains ongoing and that no revised action date has been provided. Shares fell roughly 18% on the news.

A Long Road to This Point

The missed PDUFA date marks the latest setback in an extended regulatory journey for molgramostim. The FDA had originally set an August 22, 2026 target date, then extended the review by three months to November 22 after treating Savara’s responses to information requests as a major amendment to the BLA — a standard procedural step that triggers an automatic extension but does not indicate safety or efficacy concerns. The November deadline was itself a reset following an earlier refuse-to-file letter in 2024, when the FDA initially declined to review the application due to incomplete chemistry, manufacturing, and controls data. Savara addressed those issues and resubmitted.

data.title: <![CDATA[FDA Approves Cogent Biosciences’ Ekitna for Advanced GIST, Doubling Progression-Free Survival]]>
data.description:
The US Food and Drug Administration has approved bezuclastinib (Ekitna), a selective KIT kinase inhibitor from Cogent Biosciences, in combination with sunitinib for adults with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) previously treated with imatinib. The November 24 approval, which came through the FDA’s Real-Time Oncology Review program, marks the first new treatment option for this patient population in years.

Pivotal trial delivers striking results

The approval was supported by data from the PEAK trial (NCT05208047), a randomized, open-label, international Phase III study enrolling 413 patients with GIST that had progressed on or was intolerable to imatinib. Patients received either bezuclastinib 600 mg plus sunitinib 37.5 mg orally once daily, or sunitinib alone.

The results were compelling. Median progression-free survival reached 16.5 months in the combination arm compared to 9.2 months with sunitinib alone — a 50% reduction in the risk of progression or death (hazard ratio 0.50; p<0.0001). The objective response rate was 46% with the combination versus 26% with sunitinib monotherapy (p<0.0001). Overall survival data were not yet mature at the time of the PFS analysis.

data.title: <![CDATA[Restoring the American Biotech Edge, Part 1: The Erosion]]>
data.description: We are on the eve of the greatest era of medical science in human history. Artificial intelligence is compressing target discovery, structure prediction, and molecular design. That compression should unlock the most productive period American biotechnology has ever seen. But science is not medicine. Someone must translate it. Who will lead that race: the country that invented the biotechnology industry, or a new entrant?
